title: Sabbath for the Land and the Year of Jubilee
summary: Every seventh year the land is to rest, unsown and unharvested, with its natural growth left for everyone. Every fiftieth year, the Jubilee, is announced by the ram's horn on the Day of Atonement: land returns to the families who first held it, and Israelites who sold themselves into service go free. Because the land belongs to God and the Israelites are his servants, land may not be sold permanently, poor relatives must be redeemed, loans to the poor carry no interest, and no Israelite may be ruled harshly.
story: The calendar of chapter 23 set out holy days and weeks. Chapter 25 extends the Sabbath pattern to years: a Sabbath for the land every seventh year and a great release after seven times seven years. The chapter opens by noting that God spoke these words "on Mount Sinai" (verse 1), which ties the economic laws of Israel to the covenant made there. It brings the Holiness Code to a practical climax: holiness means not only worship and sexual purity but also how land is owned, how debt is handled, and how the poor are treated. Chapter 26 follows with the blessings and curses that seal the covenant, and it recalls these Sabbath years when it warns of exile.
historical:
Many ancient Near Eastern kings proclaimed releases from debt, often at the start of a reign. The Old Babylonian Edict of Ammi-saduqa, from about the seventeenth century BC, cancelled certain debts and freed people held for debt. The Akkadian word for such a release, anduraru, is related to the Hebrew word for liberty in verse 10. Israel's law differed in making release a fixed part of the calendar, commanded by God rather than granted at a king's pleasure.

Whether the Jubilee was ever regularly observed is uncertain, and scholars differ. The Old Testament contains no clear record of a Jubilee being proclaimed. The seventh-year release fared somewhat better: Jeremiah 34 tells of King Zedekiah proclaiming liberty to Hebrew slaves during the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem, only for their owners to take them back. Second Chronicles 36:21 interprets the exile as the land at last receiving the Sabbaths it had been denied. After the return, the people pledged to keep the seventh year (Nehemiah 10:31), and 1 Maccabees records food shortages during a siege in the second century BC because it was a Sabbath year. Some scholars regard the Jubilee as an idealized law never fully practiced; others think it was kept at times but not recorded. Either way, it shaped Israel's hope, and in modern times the wording of verse 10 was cast on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia.
cultural:
In an agricultural society, land was life. A family that lost its land lost its livelihood and often its freedom, since the only thing left to sell was its own labor. When crops failed or debts mounted, a farmer might sell part of his land, then all of it, then himself or his children into service. Chapter 25 sets up three lines of defense against that slide. First, a close relative, the kinsman-redeemer, could buy back the land or the person. Second, the poor person could redeem himself if he prospered. Third, the Jubilee returned land and freed Israelite servants whether or not anyone redeemed them. The price of land was set by the number of harvests left before the Jubilee, so a buyer was really leasing the crops, not buying the land (verses 15 and 16).

The laws distinguish between kinds of property and people. Houses in walled cities, more like trade goods than family farms, could be redeemed for only a year. Village houses, tied to the fields around them, returned at the Jubilee. The Levites, who had no tribal land, always kept the right to redeem their houses. An Israelite who sold himself was to be treated as a hired worker, not a slave, because every Israelite already belonged to God as his servant. Foreigners, however, could be bought as slaves and held permanently (verses 44 to 46), a distinction discussed below.
literary: The chapter is built on the number seven: six years of work and a seventh of rest, then seven weeks of years leading to the fiftieth. The laws move outward in steps of increasing poverty: first a man sells land (verses 25 to 28), then houses (verses 29 to 34), then he cannot support himself and needs a loan (verses 35 to 38), then he sells himself to an Israelite (verses 39 to 46), and finally to a foreigner (verses 47 to 54). At each step the law provides a way back. Two refrains carry the theology: God brought Israel out of Egypt (verses 38, 42, and 55), and the land and the people belong to him (verses 23 and 55). The chapter ends where it begins, with God's ownership: "For the Israelites are My servants."

outline.t: A Sabbath year for the land
The Year of Jubilee and fair dealing
Israelites as hired workers, not slaves
Redeeming an Israelite sold to a foreigner

doctrines.note: "The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine" (verse 23). God is the owner; Israel holds the land as his tenants. That claim limits every human claim to property and makes economic life answerable to him.

Redemption in this chapter is concrete: a relative pays to restore a poor man's land or freedom. The same vocabulary describes God's rescue of Israel from Egypt and later becomes a central way the Bible describes salvation.

Verses 20 to 22 answer the obvious worry about resting the land: God promises a harvest in the sixth year large enough to last until the new crop. Keeping the Sabbath year required trusting that provision.

words.note: Yovel, a ram's horn, and so the year announced by its blast. The English word Jubilee comes from it through Latin, where it was influenced by a verb meaning to shout for joy. The Jubilee began on the Day of Atonement, so that release in the land followed cleansing before God.

Ga'al, to redeem, to buy back what was lost. The redeemer (go'el) was the nearest relative, responsible for restoring a family member's land or freedom, as Boaz does for Naomi and Ruth. The prophets, especially Isaiah, call God Israel's Redeemer, the relative who pays to set his people free.

Deror, liberty or release. It is used in verse 10 for the Jubilee proclamation, in Jeremiah 34 for the release of slaves, and in Isaiah 61:1 for the anointed one's proclamation of liberty to captives, the passage Jesus read in Nazareth.

Eved, servant or slave. The same word covers a king's officials, household slaves, and worshipers of God. Verses 42 and 55 turn it into a theological claim: Israelites are God's servants, so they cannot be the permanent slaves of anyone else.

christ: Jesus began his public ministry in Nazareth by reading Isaiah 61, a passage that draws on the Jubilee: "He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor" (Luke 4:18-19). Then he said, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:21). The Gospels present his healing, forgiveness, and welcome of the poor as the arrival of the release that the Jubilee pictured. The kinsman-redeemer also shapes the New Testament's language. Paul writes that God sent his Son, "born under the law, to redeem those under the law" (Galatians 4:4-5), and Hebrews says Jesus shared our flesh and blood and "is not ashamed to call them brothers" (Hebrews 2:11), so that he might "free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death" (Hebrews 2:15). The link between the go'el and Christ is thematic, not a direct prediction, but the pattern is strong: the near relative who pays to set the family free.

hard.q: Why does this chapter forbid enslaving Israelites but allow permanent slavery of foreigners?
hard.a: Verses 44 to 46 permit Israelites to buy slaves from the surrounding nations and from foreigners living among them, and to hold them for life and pass them on as property. Readers should face this plainly. In the nineteenth century, defenders of slavery in the United States cited these verses, while abolitionists appealed to the image of God in every person, the exodus, and the New Testament. Interpreters today offer several responses. Many argue that the law regulated an institution universal in the ancient world rather than creating it, and that the Old Testament limited it in ways unusual for its time: kidnapping a person to sell was a capital crime (Exodus 21:16), a slave injured by his master went free (Exodus 21:26-27), and a runaway slave was not to be returned (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). Some compare it to divorce, which Jesus said Moses permitted because of hardness of heart (Matthew 19:8), a concession rather than an ideal. Others stress that the chapter's own logic, that people belong to God and not to one another, points beyond the distinction it draws, and that the New Testament declares "neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free" in Christ (Galatians 3:28) and condemns "slave traders" (1 Timothy 1:10). None of these responses makes the verses easy. They do show why most Christians came to see chattel slavery as incompatible with the whole witness of Scripture.

questions: The land belonged to God, and Israel held it as his tenants. How would treating your money, home, and possessions as God's change the way you use them?
The Sabbath year required trusting God to provide without working the land. Where does rest require you to trust that you are not the one holding everything together?
The Jubilee kept families from falling into permanent poverty. What might it look like for a community today to build ways back for people who have lost everything?
